docs.title: openDendro
docs.text:
Open-source software for tree-ring science. Crossdate, detrend and build chronologies in R, in Python, or in a web browser, and keep a record that lets anyone repeat the work.

Try the apps dplR (R users) dplPy (Python users)

docs.title: What's Here
docs.text:
App · runs in the browser xDateR Crossdate a collection. Find the flagged segments, see where a ring is missing or false, fix it, and date floating series. App · runs in the browser iDetrend Detrend one series at a time. Watch the curve move as you change it and see what each choice does to the chronology. R package · on CRAN dplR The Dendrochronology Program Library in R. Read, check, crossdate, detrend, build chronologies and analyze them. Python package · prerelease on PyPI dplPy The same methods in Python, on pandas data frames, with its own documentation and worked notebooks. Book · free online Learning to Love dplR How to do tree-ring analysis in R, and why each method behaves the way it does. History COFECHA, ARSTAN and the DPL The Fortran programs these methods come from, the people who wrote them, and how we use them now.

New in October 2026

  • xDateR searches for the lag that fixes a flagged segment, checks your data on the way in, and lets you insert rings, delete rings and fill gaps.
  • iDetrend is rewritten from scratch.
  • Both apps come with guided examples, and both write a report with the R code that reproduces your work.
  • dplR 1.8.0 is on CRAN. It is a large release, and two changes can affect old scripts.
  • dplPy 0.8.0 is a solid prerelease on the way to 1.0.

docs.title: What openDendro Is
docs.text:
Dendrochronology runs on a small set of programs. For decades those were COFECHA, ARSTAN and the rest of the Dendrochronology Program Library, written in Fortran by Richard Holmes and Ed Cook and kept alive by a handful of volunteers.

openDendro is where that toolkit continues in open languages: dplR in R and dplPy in Python, with apps for the two jobs that are better done by eye, crossdating and detrending. Everything is free, and the source is on GitHub.

Three things matter to us.

Your work can be repeated. A script or a notebook is a record of what you did. The apps keep that record for you, and every report they write carries code that rebuilds the result from the original file. The choices are yours. Where a careful analyst could go either way, the software gives you an argument with a default we can defend and a help page that says what it trades. When a method cannot be applied to a series, the software stops and names the series. The old programs are a reference, not a target. We read the original Fortran to learn what a step does and why. We do not tune our code until its numbers match. More on that.

docs.title: Who We Are
docs.text:
openDendro is led by Andy Bunn (Western Washington University), Kevin Anchukaitis (University of Arizona), Tyson Swetnam (University of New Mexico) and Ed Cook (Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory), with the Paleoclimate program of the US National Science Foundation behind it. The About page has the developers, the awards and how to cite the software.

Found a bug, or want something the software doesn't do? Tell us.

docs.title: Why It Exists
docs.text:
For decades, much of the software used in dendrochronology was written in Fortran and maintained by a very small number of volunteers. As computing moves on, those programs get harder to compile and harder to run. This is the "some random person in Nebraska" problem, after the xkcd cartoon. In our field the random person is Ed Cook.

openDendro started in 2021 to move that toolkit into open languages, spread the work of maintaining it across more people, and make it usable by anyone who works with tree-ring data, in or out of dendrochronology.

docs.title: What It Includes
docs.text:
• dplR, the R package.
  • dplPy, the Python package.
  • xDateR and iDetrend, apps for crossdating and detrending in a browser.
  • Learning to Love dplR, a free book.

All of it is open source and on GitHub.

docs.title: How We Work
docs.text:
• Judge a method by what it does to the data. The question for any step is its effect on the series and on the conclusions drawn from them.
  • Turn choices into arguments. Where a careful analyst could go either way, the choice is an argument with a default we can defend and documentation of what it trades.
  • Say what was done. Output records the settings used. A function does not quietly swap one method for another.
  • Fail loudly. When a method cannot be applied to a series, the software stops or warns and names the series.
  • Keep reading the source. COFECHA and ARSTAN are where these methods come from. We read them, cite them and credit the people who wrote them. We do not treat a difference from them as a defect. More on that.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
Most of openDendro is meant to be used from a script, because a script is a record of what was done. Two jobs are better done by eye: crossdating and detrending. You need to look at each series, try something, and look again.

These Shiny apps do those two jobs in a web browser. There is nothing to install. Both are built on dplR, and both keep the record for you: every report has R code that reproduces your results from the original file.

Each app comes with example data and guided walk-throughs. Look for "Show me how" in the sidebar.

docs.title: xDateR
docs.text:
Open xDateR Source on GitHub

xDateR is for checking the dating of a collection and fixing it. If you have used COFECHA, the segment correlations and the flags will look familiar.

  • See the whole collection at once. Each series is cut into overlapping segments and correlated against a master built from the others. Segments that fit poorly are flagged.
  • Find the lag. Each segment is also tested a few years either side of where it is dated. A segment that fits better somewhere else is marked, with a hint on whether to look for a missing ring or a false one, and where.
  • Fix it. Insert a ring, delete a ring or fill a gap, and watch the correlations respond. Edits can be undone one at a time.
  • Check the data first. Data Checks on the Overview say in plain language what needs a look.
  • Date floating series. Compare the candidate positions for an undated series against a dated master and choose one.

The statistics say where to look. The wood says what happened. Go back to the sample before you accept an edit.

docs.title: iDetrend
docs.text:
Open iDetrend Source on GitHub

iDetrend is for choosing a detrending curve for each series while you look at it. The app was rewritten for dplR 1.8.0.

  • See a curve move as you change its rigidity, with the indices drawn underneath.
  • Compare methods on one series, with the curves laid over each other.
  • See the series against the stand. The mean of the other series sits behind each one, so you can tell a swing the trees share from one this tree has alone.
  • Be told what a setting does. Under a spline's controls the app says, in years, which swings in growth it removes and which it keeps.
  • Be told where to look. A series whose curve fell back to another method, or runs close to zero, is marked with the reason.
  • See what your choices did. The chronology and its statistics are shown beside the same data detrended with dplR's defaults.
  • Pick up where you stopped. A settings file restores the work in a later session.

iDetrend fits curves to single series. It does not do regional curve or signal-free standardization. Use rcs and ssf in dplR for those.

docs.title: Running the Apps on Your Own Computer
docs.text:
The hosted apps are the easy way in. If you would like to run one locally, say to work offline or on data you can't upload, you need R and dplR 1.8.0 or later:

install.packages(c("shiny", "dplR"))
shiny::runGitHub("xDateR", "OpenDendro")
shiny::runGitHub("iDetrend", "OpenDendro")

R will tell you if another package is missing. Each app's README on GitHub says how to restore the exact package versions it was built with.

docs.title: treeSong
docs.text:
Source on GitHub

treeSong turns the spectral properties of a tree-ring series into sound. It is an experiment in hearing a time series as well as plotting it. Because it plays audio, it runs best on your own computer:

install.packages("shiny")
shiny::runGitHub("treeSong", "OpenDendro")

docs.title: The Programs
docs.text:
Two Fortran programs defined how the field crossdates and standardizes tree-ring data.

COFECHA was written by the late Richard Holmes at the University of Arizona's Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research. It checks the dating of a collection by correlating each series, in segments, against a master built from the others. Holmes also wrote the Dendrochronology Program Library (the DPL), the set of utilities that grew up around it.

ARSTAN was written by Ed Cook at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. It detrends ring-width series, models their autocorrelation, and builds the standard, residual and ARSTAN chronologies.

Paul Krusic, Ed's long-time collaborator, has worked on both programs with him for years.

For signal-free standardization, the reference is CRUST, by Tom Melvin and Keith Briffa at the Climatic Research Unit.

docs.title: Where to Get Them
docs.text:
• Dendro software from Lamont-Doherty, hosted at Cambridge.
  • Software at the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research.
  • CRUST on GitHub.

docs.title: A Reference, Not a Target
docs.text:
dplR, dplPy and the openDendro apps come out of these programs. They are no longer checked against them.

COFECHA and ARSTAN were written for a terminal and a menu of numbered options. A program in that setting had to make most decisions for the person using it, and it did. Those decisions were choices, and some were argued over by the authors themselves. Ed Cook argued against making the log transform COFECHA's default. It stayed the default anyway.

Matching the old numbers means adopting the old choices whether or not they suit the data at hand. On one collection, a series' correlation with the master averaged 0.09 higher in dplR than in COFECHA. Nearly all of that traced to two COFECHA steps that dplR does not take, a log transform and a variance stabilization. Neither program was wrong. Closing the gap would have meant adopting both steps because COFECHA has them, which is not a reason.

So the original Fortran stays open on the desk. We read it to learn what a step does and why it was done. Where our result differs from ARSTAN or COFECHA, the documentation says which step causes it, so that someone coming from those programs knows what changed.

Some things do not change:

  • A negative crossdating lag means a missing ring in the series, as it does in COFECHA.
  • Tucson and the other legacy file formats are read and written faithfully. Decades of data are stored in them.
  • Where an older program's approach is a reasonable choice, it is offered as an option.

openDendro exists because Richard Holmes, Ed Cook, Paul Krusic and others wrote these programs and shared them.

docs.title: dplPy
docs.text:
dplPy is the Dendrochronology Program Library in Python. It brings the methods of dplR to Python and works on pandas data frames: read and write ring-width files, summarize, detrend, build chronologies, crossdate, date floating series, and do regional curve standardization.

dplPy is in prerelease, at version 0.8.0 and heading for 1.0. It is ready to use, and function names and arguments can still change before 1.0.

dplPy documentation Source on GitHub

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dplPy needs Python 3.10 or later.

pip install dplpy

The installation guide covers setting up Python and an environment if you are starting from nothing.

docs.title: A First Chronology
docs.text:
import dplpy as dpl

rwl = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl", header=True)   # ring widths, one column per series
dpl.stats(rwl)                                # summary statistics for each series
rwi = dpl.detrend(rwl, fit="spline")          # ring-width indices
crn = dpl.chron(rwi)                          # the chronology

The quickstart takes this file from raw ring widths to a crossdated chronology, with the output of every step.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
• The dplPy documentation has a guide for each task and a reference for every function.
  • Coming from dplR is for people who already know the R package.
  • Fidelity and departures says where dplPy matches dplR and the Fortran programs, how that is checked, and where it differs on purpose.
  • The notebooks on this site are worked examples you can download and run: an introduction, a floating chronology, a bristlecone pine collection, and pulling data from the ITRDB.

docs.title: Bugs and Requests
docs.text: dplPy is young and gets better when people break it. Report a bug or ask for a feature on the dplPy issue tracker.

docs.title: dplR
docs.text: dplR is the Dendrochronology Program Library in R. It reads and writes the standard tree-ring formats, checks a collection for problems, crossdates, detrends, builds chronologies and analyzes them. It is on CRAN and is the R side of openDendro.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install R, then:

install.packages("dplR")
library(dplR)

That gives you the released version from CRAN.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
Learning to Love dplR is a free online book on doing tree-ring analysis with dplR. It covers how to call the functions, what each method is doing, and when a method misleads. Start there.

The package also has a vignette, "Getting Started with dplR", and a help page for every function.

If you would sooner point and click for crossdating or detrending, the apps run dplR in a web browser and hand you the R code afterwards.

docs.title: New in 1.8.0
docs.text:
1.8.0 is a large release. The highlights:

  • rwl.check looks for defects in a collection: duplicate or empty series, gaps, zeros, units errors and dating errors.
  • xdate.report writes a COFECHA-style crossdating report, with flags and the lag that would fix each flagged segment.
  • corr.rwl.seg can test each segment at shifted dates and return the best lag.
  • read.sheet and write.sheet read and write spreadsheet-shaped files.
  • Ring-width indices and basal area increments have their own classes, so a function can warn when it is handed the wrong kind of series.

Two changes can affect old scripts

  • read.tucson no longer fills a gap inside a series with zeros. A gap is now NA, and functions that reject NA inside a series will stop until you fill the gap on purpose.
  • detrend now defaults to method = "Spline". The old default ran every method and returned a list.

Read the NEWS file before you update.

docs.title: Bristlecone Pine Example
docs.text:
This notebook uses raw ring widths for bristlecone pine (Pinus longaeva) at Campito Mountain in California, USA. This is one of the datasets included in dplR as well and include in the dplPy distribution.

Graybill, D. A. and LaMarche, Jr., V. C. (1983) Campito Mountain Data Set. IGBP PAGES/World Data Center for Paleoclimatology Data Contribution Series 1983-CA533.RWL. NOAA/NCDC Paleoclimatology Program, Boulder, Colorado, USA: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/paleo/treering/measurements/northamerica/usa/ca533.rwl

Let's start by importing some standard Python libraries. We'll bring in Pandas (for working with 2 dimensional data), Matplotlib to help with plotting,

In [ ]: Copied! 
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 

# the following two lines nicely render figures in the notebook 
%config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina'
%matplotlib inline

# you can omit the line below if you'd like, but I really don't like the default fonts in Python, so I switch to Helvetica
plt.rcParams['font.family'] = 'Helvetica'
plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (10, 5)
import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # the following two lines nicely render figures in the notebook %config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina' %matplotlib inline # you can omit the line below if you'd like, but I really don't like the default fonts in Python, so I switch to Helvetica plt.rcParams['font.family'] = 'Helvetica' plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (10, 5)

We can update (or install) dplpy directly from this notebook if necessary using the 'bang' (!) command - you can just skip this code block or comment it out if you're already running the latest version from the Pypi repository.

In [ ]: Copied! 
# if necessary, install dplpy
# !pip install dplpy

# if necessary upgrade dplpy to the latest version, v0.1.2 as of January 8th, 2024
# !pip install dplpy --upgrade
# if necessary, install dplpy # !pip install dplpy # if necessary upgrade dplpy to the latest version, v0.1.2 as of January 8th, 2024 # !pip install dplpy --upgrade

Let us now import dplpy and we'll check the version number and see where the library is on our system. If everything is working well, the codeblock should complete without error and you should see that you are running v0.1.2 from one of your Python directories (you will see /envs/ in the path if you are in a virtual environment)

In [ ]: Copied! 
import dplpy as dpl

# print out the version number of dplPy you are using - should be v0.1.2 
print('Currently using the following version of dplPy:', dpl.__version__)

# You should see the path to your local Python installation
print('Currently using the following directory for dplPy:', dpl.__file__)
import dplpy as dpl # print out the version number of dplPy you are using - should be v0.1.2 print('Currently using the following version of dplPy:', dpl.__version__) # You should see the path to your local Python installation print('Currently using the following directory for dplPy:', dpl.__file__)

Let's read the Campito Mountain raw measurement series into our notebook now. We will use the dpl.readers method to do this. For the moment, .readers automatically identified the file type from the file suffix, looking for .rwl for Tucson formatted decadal files, or .csv. In the future, the method will recognize a wider variety of suffixes (e.g. .raw), allow you to pass the file type directly to the method, or pull from the ITRDB.

In [ ]: Copied! 
# Read in the Campito Mountain series and assign to a variable
ca533 = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl")
# Read in the Campito Mountain series and assign to a variable ca533 = dpl.readers("ca533.rwl") In [ ]: Copied! 
# take a look at the DataFrame
ca533 #1358 years by 34 columns
# take a look at the DataFrame ca533 #1358 years by 34 columns

We could also read in the Sheep Mountain update (ca667.rwl). This file has headers, though - we tell .readers about the existence of the Tucson style (3 line) headers when we call .readers:

In [ ]: Copied! 
# Can specify whether file has headers so reading of data is done appropriately
ca667 = dpl.readers("ca667.rwl", header=True)
ca667 # 310 columns, 4655 years
# Can specify whether file has headers so reading of data is done appropriately ca667 = dpl.readers("ca667.rwl", header=True) ca667 # 310 columns, 4655 years In [ ]: Copied! 
print(ca533.index) # Campito Mountain chronology covers 626 to 1983
print(ca667.index)  # Campito Mountain chronology covers -2649 (BCE) to 2005!
print(ca533.index) # Campito Mountain chronology covers 626 to 1983 print(ca667.index) # Campito Mountain chronology covers -2649 (BCE) to 2005!

We could, if we wanted, use Pandas to merge the two datasets to form a combined Sheep-Campito Mountain chronology. The codeblock below shows how to use Pandas .merge to do this. Because this creates a very large and very long set of series, we won't use this in the rest of the notebook, but it is useful to see how you might do this. Of note is that the .merge function is NOT unique to dplpy - following the overall philosophy also adopted for dplR, we don't create functions with openDendro to do common data manipulations or data handling (e.g. things that are not specific to dendrochronology):

In [ ]: Copied! 
shpcmp = pd.merge(ca533, ca667, left_index=True, right_index=True, how='outer') # this is just a pure Pandas command
shpcmp # pretty-print from Pandas will show 4655 years x 344 columns
shpcmp = pd.merge(ca533, ca667, left_index=True, right_index=True, how='outer') # this is just a pure Pandas command shpcmp # pretty-print from Pandas will show 4655 years x 344 columns

Back to Campito Mountain (ca533)now. Our dplpy provides both .summary statistics (the individual series mean, quantiles, max and min values) as well as the .statistics of the individual series including first and last year, mean, median, standard deviation, skew, gini coefficient and AR1 coefficient similar to ARSTAN. The module names follow those in dplR and report complementary data:

In [ ]: Copied! 
dpl.summary(ca533)
dpl.summary(ca533) In [ ]: Copied! 
dpl.stats(ca533)
dpl.stats(ca533)

Another module available is the .report, which has information similar to that provided by COFECHA and mirrors the similar function in dplR, including the years with locally absent rings in each individual series:

In [ ]: Copied!

docs.title: About¶
docs.text:
The NCEI Paleo Web Service is searchable via its web interface:https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/paleo-search/

Here we are using its API: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/paleo-search/api

Specifically, we are interested in Tree Ring Data

docs.title: Tutorial 1: Using Python to access the API for tree ring .rwl data¶
Step 1: Activate/Create a Python environment¶
docs.text:
First, you need to import the necessary libraries in Python. The most common ones used for API calls are requests for making HTTP requests and json for handling JSON data.

We also want to plot the data using maplotlib, numpy, and pandas which are all core libraries for scientific Python.

Later, we will use fiona and Leaflet maps to visualize the site locations.

docs.title: Step 2: Set the base url for the API as api_base¶
docs.text: Define the base url to the NOAA Paleoclimate API, this URL is the starting point for all future requests.

docs.title: Step 3: Search via API for tree ring (dataTypeID=18) studies of raw ring width.¶
docs.text:
Returns pages of 10 studies at a time. Set this limit to avoid overwhelming the API with large requests.

Results are returned in JSON format as a dict called "data".

Note, when searching via the user interface, the API call used to retrieve results is displayed immediately above the search results and can be used to generate a "req_str" relevant to the use case.

docs.title: Request the entire JSON response¶
docs.text:
Now that we have previewed the API and are satisfied with the response, we are going to re-run the code from above, but this time, we want the entire response, not just the headers.

Also, we are going to increase our limit request from limit=10 to limit=500 sites.

Note: we have removed &headersOnly=true from our req_params, the api_base request is unchanged.

docs.title: Viewing the API output on a map¶
Step 4: install Python library folium¶
docs.text:
We need to install folium maps and its required dependencies into our Python environment. This can be done by using an environment.yml (see provided example), or by installing on the fly using conda, mamba, or pip

mamba install -c conda-forge folium

docs.title: Step 5: Plot the locations of the API results on an interactive map¶
docs.text:
Create a base folium map, in our example we are zoomed in and centered over North America.

Next, we call the JSON data response from the API.

The JSON contains the geo geometric coordinates of the study area and its point location

In the map, we are tagging the doi, the Site Name and Site ID.

Optionally, if the file has a .rwl, a .pdf, or .png fire history figure associated with it, we provide a hyperlink.

On Mac OS X, press the command button ⌘ and click on the hyperlink to open in your browser.

If you click the link directly it may open in the Notebook widget. To go back, just re-run the notebook cell
